source.title: The power of fine-grained experts: Granularity boosts expressivity in Mixture of Experts

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The experiments test whether an architectural choice changes model loss, using student-to-teacher fitting of synthetic MoE models rather than language-model pretraining loss or a scaling-law sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior empirical MoE scaling-law results, including Krajewski et al., but does not report those results as its own. Its own experiments report teacher-student fitting outcomes and bear on V4; they do not test the power-law, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream-predictability versions.
record.test_reason: No version is tested. The experiments train small synthetic MoE students to regress random MoE teachers with MSE on Gaussian inputs, not language-model pretraining loss. Teachers are built with a given granularity, so the setup measures expressivity (can a student represent the target), not how architecture shape affects language-model loss at fixed size. The theory is an expressivity separation. The scaling-law link is only cited agreement with Krajewski et al. This is a related construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove that higher MoE granularity gives an exponential expressivity gain at fixed active parameters. Their experiments show students fit teachers of similar or lower granularity but not higher. They recommend higher granularity, subject to routing and hardware costs, and note optimisation by SGD as an open question.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theoretical expressivity separations and synthetic student-teacher fitting with mean-squared error, not language-model pretraining sweeps measuring held-out cross-entropy or fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Student-teacher fit depends on granularity; the Figure 3 experiment includes trainable routing-vector bias, and the authors report optimization difficulty without that bias. They also select the better fit from two learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic teacher-student MoE regression (d=256, about 65K active teacher parameters), students with lower granularity than the teacher fail to fit it, even with 16x total parameters. Students of equal or higher granularity fit to about 0 MSE. A theorem proves an exponential expressivity separation in granularity at fixed active parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed active and total parameters, MoE granularity (number of active experts) strongly changes expressivity and achievable fit, so it is not a minor shape detail for MoE architectures.

record.problems: The experiments use synthetic MoE teacher-student fitting with mean-squared error rather than language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The paper notes optimization difficulties and reports selecting the better result from two learning rates.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2's numerical entries were not recorded separately because the extracted layout does not unambiguously map all flattened values to architectures; the paper's aggregate textual result is recorded in r1. Figure 3's plot-only numerical values were not extracted; its stated aggregate outcome is recorded in r2.

untested.parts: Effect of shape (including MoE granularity) on held-out language-model pretraining loss at fixed parameter count; only synthetic teacher-student fitting is run.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's label (V4 challenges) is dropped. The system and measure differ from V4's language-model pretraining loss, and the teachers are constructed to require granularity. The text cites Krajewski et al.'s empirical granularity scaling laws as agreeing, but these are not the study's own results. Student selection picks the better of two learning rates.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
The experiments test sensitivity to MoE granularity in synthetic teacher-student fitting, not depth and width variation generally or held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Student MoE models (aggregate across tested architectures)
rows.size_stated: Teachers have approximately 65K active parameters; students have approximately 82K active parameters.
rows.stage_stated: Student models trained to learn random teacher MoE models; not language-model pretraining.
rows.operation_detail: Train students to fit teacher MoE models while varying granularity at fixed total and active parameter counts.

conditions.value: Total and active parameter counts fixed across the Figure 2 comparison
Teacher and student granularity varied across tested architectures
Two learning rates in {0.01, 0.001}; report the better fit

rows.value: The paper states that the student model must match the teacher's granularity in order to learn.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the tested teacher-student architecture comparisons. The extracted Figure 2 numerical entries are flattened and their cell-to-architecture mapping is not sufficiently clear to record individually.
rows.check: The subject is synthetic MoE regressors on Gaussian data fitted to random MoE teachers, not language-model pretraining loss, so the row does not measure what V4 names. The value is also incomplete. In Figure 2, students with granularity at or above the teacher's reach about 0.00 loss, and lower-granularity students do not (e.g. 32e16a teacher: 0.23 down to 0.00). Section 5 says students fit teachers of 'similar or lower granularity', not only matching ones. The caption's 'teacher trained to learn a student' wording is a typo for the reverse.

rows.subject: Student MoE models (aggregate across tested architectures)
rows.size_stated: Teacher is a 16-expert, 8-active-expert model; students include models up to 16 times the teacher's total size. Teachers have approximately 65K active parameters and students approximately 82K active parameters.
rows.stage_stated: Student models trained to learn a teacher MoE model; not language-model pretraining.
rows.operation_detail: Train students of varying granularity and total parameter count to fit a fixed teacher.

conditions.value: Up to 16 times teacher total size
Trainable bias added to routing vectors

rows.value: The paper states that even students up to 16 times as large do not fit the teacher unless student granularity is at least 8.
rows.note: The paper reports the outcome in aggregate; no numerical loss values are stated in the accompanying text.
rows.check: Same construct mismatch: student-teacher MSE fit, not language-model loss. Students had a trainable routing bias. Without it, the authors could not optimise students even at granularity 8, so the outcome depends on the optimisation setup.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Tested synthetic MoE teacher-student fitting settings
reader_labels.reason: Granularity changes whether students fit their teachers, including when parameter count is increased substantially; this is not a small loss effect in the tested settings (r1, r2).
